Anthropic closed day 2 at $88.30, down 9% from Thursday and 6% above its $83 IPO price.

Its low of $83.05 came 5 cents above the IPO price before a 6% bounce into the close.

Facebook (2012) and Uber (2019) both closed day 2 below their IPO prices, by 10% and 18%; Arm (2023) stayed 19% above.

Released: The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income. It is a free guide from Fisher Investments covering what your retirement will really cost, where the cash flow should come from, and how much you can safely withdraw each year. Learn more here. Learn More Here › (sponsor)

Anthropic (NASDAQ: ANT) closed its second day of trading on Friday at $88.30, down 9% from Thursday's close of $97.17. At its low of the day it traded at $83.05, 5 cents above its $83 IPO price, then bounced 6% into the close.

The stock finished 6% above the price IPO buyers paid. It's 23% below Thursday's high of $115.10.

24/7 Wall St.

Anthropic was down almost 10% before the bell as AI and chip stocks sold off for a second day. Nvidia fell 12% after Reuters reported an SEC probe of its accounting, and Broadcom fell 12% after a report that Google cut its plans for Broadcom AI chips. The Nasdaq 100 was down about 4% for much of the afternoon.

How other big tech IPOs did on day 2

Facebook priced at $38 in 2012. On its second day it fell 11% and closed at $34.03, 10% below its IPO price. It didn't close back above $38 until Aug. 2, 2013.

Uber priced at $45 in 2019 and opened below it. On day 2 it fell another 11% to $37.10, 18% below its IPO price.

Arm priced at $51 in 2023. It fell 4% on its second day and closed at $60.75, still 19% above its IPO price. A year later it traded well above that.

Why $83 matters

The IPO price is what the underwriters' clients paid before trading began. Underwriters sometimes buy shares near that price in the first days to support it, and traders watch it as a floor. On Friday the floor held, by 5 cents.

Bitcoin is priced at $59,445, having dropped 5.8% in the past 24 hours and 32.1% this year. This price puts Bitcoin 52.9% below its peak of $126,080 and just 1.5% above the one-year low of $58,566 recorded on June 30.

Anthropic, known for developing the Claude chatbot, priced its IPO at $83 per share, exceeding the initial range of $70 to $78. The company raised $81.3 billion at a valuation around $1.5 trillion. Shares opened at roughly $112, peaked at $115, and closed their first day at $97, meaning a $1,000 investment buys about 10 shares.

However, the stock fell about 14% in its second trading session, leading a wider sell-off in AI stocks that pushed the Nasdaq down for the year. The X account DeItaone posted on November 17 that Bitcoin's losses were mounting as investors shifted their focus to the Anthropic IPO, a link Grok AI also drew in its take on what the record IPO could mean for Bitcoin.

title: “Pretty Bizarre”: Microsoft Is Worth More Than Alphabet. Which Makes No Sense
detail:
“Pretty Bizarre”: Microsoft Is Worth More Than Alphabet. Which Makes No Sense
Michael Douglass
Fri, November 20, 2026 at 1:38 PM MST 5 min read
GOOGN
MSFT
META
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
"Pretty Bizarre": Microsoft Is Worth More Than Alphabet. Which Makes No Sense ©@aukidphumsirichat via Canva, @champpixs from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Alphabet hit a 52-week low, leaving it worth $3.34 trillion against Microsoft's $3.70 trillion.

Analysts expect Alphabet to earn about $172 billion over the next 12 months, against about $154 billion for Microsoft.

Amazon and Microsoft trade near 25x forward earnings, while Meta and Alphabet trade near 18x to 19x, even though Google Cloud grew 103% last quarter.

I'd rather own Alphabet, with search growth and 2027 spending plans in its early-February report as the test.

Alphabet (GOOG) hit a 52-week low this week. It's down 20% in a month and 32% below its high, which leaves it worth $3.34 trillion. Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ), just 10% off its own high, is worth $3.70 trillion.

One investor in r/ValueInvesting calls that "pretty bizarre":

"At the end of the day, the market cap is supposed to approximate the present value of the future cash flows. I have a hard time seeing Microsoft make more money than Alphabet from now until their eventual bankruptcies."

Which…yeah, agreed.

Microsoft gets the richer multiple

Microsoft trades at 24x the earnings analysts expect over the next 12 months. That's below its five-year average of 29x but well above the 19x it hit in June:

Microsoft (MSFT): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years (TIKR)

Alphabet trades at 19x, against a five-year average of 23x. It was at 33x as recently as April:

Alphabet (GOOG): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years (TIKR)

So the market has paid up for Microsoft's earnings for years. But Alphabet's earnings have caught up.

Alphabet is expected to earn more

Alphabet's profit more than doubled from 2022 to 2025:

Alphabet (GOOG): net income, $ billions, fiscal 2021-2025 (TIKR)

Its $132 billion of net income in 2025 was about level with the $133.7 billion Microsoft earned in its fiscal year ended June 2026.

From here, Alphabet pulls ahead. Divide each company's market value by its forward multiple, and you get roughly what analysts expect it to earn over the next 12 months: about $172 billion for Alphabet, against about $154 billion for Microsoft.

So investors are paying $360 billion more for the company expected to earn about $18 billion less. Bizarre.

The market is pricing Alphabet like an ad company

The market isn't treating all the big AI spenders alike. Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ) trades at 25x forward earnings, right next to Microsoft, while Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) trades at 18x, right next to Alphabet.

title: Wall Street Thinks Oklo Is a Buy. Here’s Why I’m Not So Sure.
detail:
Wall Street Thinks Oklo Is a Buy. Here’s Why I’m Not So Sure.
Ryan Vanzo, The Motley Fool
Fri, November 20, 2026 at 1:25 PM MST 3 min read
OKLO
META
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Many stocks related to the AI boom trade at premium valuations. Some, however, have seen their rich valuations cut in half or more this year. Oklo (NYSE:OKLO) is one of them.

Oklo specializes in small modular reactors, or SMRs. These nuclear energy facilities can be built more quickly than conventional nuclear power plants. Their small size also allows them to be co-located next to AI data center infrastructure.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

AI is energy-intensive. To avoid grid reliance, AI companies have invested aggressively to scale additional energy supply. Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META), for example, is partnering with Oklo on a 1.2 gigawatt SMR system in Ohio.

Despite the 70% slide in 2026, Wall Street remains upbeat on Oklo stock. No analysts currently have a "sell" rating on the stock. Several have price targets that predict more than 100% upside potential.

But here's the thing: I'm still not buying Oklo shares. And there's one reason why.

Here's why I'm not buying Oklo stock

I am a big fan of SMRs as a technology. Research from Bank of America suggests that SMRs will play a role in the world's long-term energy landscape.

The problem is that SMR scaling will likely take decades. That makes Oklo a suspect investment, even at today's prices.

Image source: Getty Images.

Oklo's business model doesn't just include manufacturing SMR systems. The company also intends to own and operate the assets. That may create more long-term revenue and profit potential. But it also makes Oklo's business model more capital-intensive.

Analysts don't expect Oklo to generate positive operating income until 2031 or 2032. That means the company will need to raise new capital for years to come. While shares are cheaper after the correction, it is now harder -- or at least more onerous for existing shareholders -- for Oklo to raise more money.

Oklo is in a strange position as an investment candidate. As shares get cheaper, it actually becomes harder for the company to finance itself -- something it will likely need to do for the rest of the decade. For that reason, I'm sticking to the sidelines for now.
